Redraw as premium Hayao Miyazaki-inspired hand-drawn Japanese animation culinary instruction art, consistent with the site's onigiri illustration reference: thin warm-brown ink contours, expressive but anatomically precise adult hands, clean matte two/three-tone cel shading, softly painted warm ivory background, muted peach skin, deep coral-red tuna, creamy white rice with a few dozen clean individually outlined grains, subtle pale honey wood only where a tabletop is needed. Clearly an animated illustration, NEVER photorealistic. No skin pores, fingerprints, photographic textures, glossy skin, 3D CGI, plastic rendering, geometric diagram hands, grids, labels, text, numbers or watermarks. Keep the food small and plausible, the instructional contacts precise, all hands anatomically complete with exactly one thumb plus four fingers, connected naturally; no extra/fused/missing digits. Use readable clear negative spaces. Orange arrows/dots only for pressure/contact; blue arcs only for motion when specified. Landscape 3:2 for steps/hero; square for ingredient cards. No text, no labels, no lettering, no watermark, no people, no animals or characters.

Rules: smooth, clean surfaces with crisp, well-defined outlines — no grain, noise, hatching, stippling, paper or crackle texture anywhere. Draw only what the scene names; nothing carried over from other steps. Food is in exactly the state the scene describes — nothing cooked, assembled or garnished ahead of time. Cooked egg is silky and glossy in soft folds, never curdled, foamy or pebbly; simmering liquid is smooth with only a few clean bubbles; rice is a soft mound with a modest number of clearly drawn grains. Cuts, sizes and quantities exactly as described and realistic. When a hand steadies food during knife work, it uses a proper claw grip (guiding fingertips tucked under, knuckles against the blade). A chicken thigh fillet is small and thin — about palm-sized (12 × 8 cm), 1–2 cm thick, irregular, pale pink with a little white fat — never a big thick slab, never marbled red like pork or beef. Hands belong to one right-handed cook seen from their own position: the right hand does the knife/chopsticks/pouring work from the right side of the frame, the left hand steadies or holds the pan handle from the left; keep the camera angle the same across a recipe's pictures. Prefer a tight close-up where the subject fills the frame. Every hand has exactly five digits: one thumb and four fingers of anatomically proportional lengths (middle longest, index and ring similar, little shortest), correct joints and thumb side. Fingers may be naturally occluded but never fused, added, elongated or truncated. Safe knife claw grip; blade cannot intersect fingers. One right-handed cook, consistent camera and vessels. Tight close-up showing the actual action and cut size. For rocking-chopping nuts, a free hand may safely rest on the blunt knife spine near the tip; never on the sharp edge.

A tight culinary close-up on a warm ivory surface, consistent low three-quarter view. Small peeled floury potato wedges, each about 6 cm long and 1.5 cm thick across its widest cut face. Deep stainless pot, ivory bowls and wire rack. No decorative props.

Scene: Mise-en-place ingredient still life: viewed from directly above (top-down), Tempura preparation ingredients in three small ivory bowls: a smooth white mound of dry tempura flour mix, a smaller smooth white mound of cornstarch, and clear cold water. No packets, no lettering, no herbs, no cooked food., centred and filling about 80% of a square frame, on a plain clean off-white background with a soft round shadow. Nothing else in frame, no hands, no table edges.

Match the approved reference exactly in line quality, hands, muted warm palette and culinary detail. The original style reference above is retained verbatim; its optional arrows are superseded: NO arrows, dots, motion arcs, diagram insets or labels. Preserve real ingredient structure with readable broad muscle lines, seeds, cut edges and folds. Sparse detail is not featureless flat blobs. Tight close-up of food and actual tool contact, filling most of the frame; plain warm ivory setting, no decorative kitchen props. No photographic textures or recursive microtexture.

How to draw small repeated things (rice grains, bubbles, crumbs, starch, flour, panko, crust nubs, sesame seeds, salt, sugar, chilli and spice flakes, bonito flakes, nori bits): draw each one INDIVIDUALLY as a distinct, separate piece — a simple clean shape with its own thin crisp outline, smooth cel shading and one small highlight, all at the same readable size (each at least about 1/80 of the picture width), like individually placed game sprites. Show a countable number — a few dozen, not hundreds. Never a dense swarm or speckled field, never clusters made of smaller clusters, never pieces shrinking into ever-tinier copies toward the edges: no fractal, self-similar, recursive, frothy, foamy, beaded, sponge-like or cauliflower-like surfaces. Where there would really be hundreds, draw the mass as one smooth flat-coloured shape and outline only a few dozen individual pieces on its surface and edges. Leave visible space between pieces — never a carpet of overlapping detailed pieces filling the frame. Small creatures (baby fish, tiny shrimp) are simplified to a clean silhouette with one eye dot — no scales, stripes or segments. Hot oil and simmering liquid: a smooth glossy surface with a dozen or so separate round bubbles, no froth. Fried crust is NOT made of pieces: a smooth, glossy, crisp shell following the food's softly lumpy shape, with a few soft creases and ridges and a handful of small flakes at its edges — never beads, dots, nubs, popcorn or cauliflower texture.
